content:
Earlier this year, I replaced a gas-powered mower with a robot mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. Users can manually drive the robot along the edge of the lawn to build a virtual map. Once set up, the robot automatically mows according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tested another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I believe this machine may be easier for many people to use.

Camera-assisted automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year is how each understands your lawn.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundary with my iPhone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. Equipped with three cameras, the mower can automatically map out the lawn area without needing boundary wires buried underground or an additional RTK antenna installed.

The automatic initial mapping process takes longer, but I think it may be simpler for people who are not very comfortable with computer technology.

To verify this, I asked my mother, who lives in another state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She said everything worked fine. That said, I'm not entirely sure whether she would have had the patience to first manually drive the robot with her phone along the entire boundary and mark out all the areas to avoid.

In my front yard, there were a few small hiccups during the automatic mapping process. There is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's, so TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's lawn in my map.

I set that area as a no-go zone in the app, and the problem was resolved. That said, if there is no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, extra care is needed when creating the initial map.

Peeking through the mower's cameras

TerraMow's cameras also enable one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a live view of what the mower sees while it is working.

During testing, I used my iPhone's screen mirroring feature to display this feed as a large window on my Mac. I could sit inside working, while watching from the mower's perspective as it moved around the back yard.

This feature is not essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun and can sometimes explain why the mower slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 does not have a corresponding camera feed feature.

Beyond that, the two iPhone apps share a lot in common. Both support preset schedules, mowing mode adjustments, zone划分, no-go zone markers, and remote control of the mower.

TerraMow has a particularly thoughtful twist on that last feature. In addition to the traditional left-right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold your iPhone normally and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone is not the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically on a preset schedule without human intervention. That said, TerraMow's joystick mode is genuinely fun for tidying up small patches the robot may have missed.

Sometimes I almost feel like I'm controlling the robot by telekinesis (the fun kind). I hold the iPhone while walking beside the mower, give a gentle push with my thumb, and the robot follows in the direction I'm steering.

Every robot mower app should copy this design.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and ran louder.

I wouldn't say TerraMow is 'noisy,' but the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot runs very quietly—quiet enough that you almost forget it's still going, even when it's out mowing at night with its headlights on.

Because TerraMow relies on camera-based navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. So scheduling daytime mowing becomes even more important.

The V1000 itself feels solidly built and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage to cover the charging dock, whereas Anthbot's garage has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, TerraMow has been consistently stable and reliable. I relied on it for daily mowing for several weeks straight, with no human intervention required at any point.

When adaptive mapping is too 'smart'

The same visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continually adjusts its map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these changes takes quite a while, during which you cannot perform other actions in the app.

After several days of heavy rain, I ran into an interesting edge case. A puddle formed in one spot in the yard, and TerraMow wisely avoided that area on its next run.

Within the skipped circular patch, the weeds grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to misinterpret the growth there as something to keep avoiding, and even after the ground dried out, the area continued to be skipped.

I used the app's remote control feature to manually drive the mower over and cut down the taller grass, and the problem was resolved. Once the area returned to normal, automatic mowing resumed there as well.

Regular edging also helps TerraMow approach boundaries more confidently. Tall grass growing along an indistinct line could otherwise be mistaken for an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more heavily on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. That method requires more upfront work, but it avoids the situation where the map 'changes its mind' about the same patch of grass.

9to5Mac Conclusion

Having used both systems, for most people I lean toward recommending TerraMow's camera-based approach.

For me, burying wires underground is completely impractical, and installing an RTK base station means placing, powering, and maintaining extra hardware. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation is not flawless. Initial mapping takes longer, fuzzy property lines need manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook a patch of overgrown weeds for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are all manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, an engaging live camera feed, and the best manual control experience of any robot mower app I've used.

I genuinely enjoy working in the yard, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing that chore over to a robot frees up time to tend to flower beds, edge, and do detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 excels at this, and I would recommend it, especially for users who want a robot mower but don't want to bury wires underground, install an RTK antenna, or walk around the entire yard holding their phone from start to finish.

Amazon currently prices the TerraMow V1000 at $999, after applying a $200 coupon code on the deal site. The product is also available for purchase on TerraMow's official website.
